content.summary_of_the_paper:
The paper considers the problem of transferring a pre-trained model from a source task to a target task. 
the paper focuses on regression tasks and develops evaluation methods for measuring the transferability between the two tasks with the pre-trained model. The paper presents generalization bounds to prove the viability of these metrics.  

The authors test their methods on several well-established datasets and against two state of the art baseline methods for transfer learning in regression settings. The comparison is done w.r.t the performance and runtime complexity.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
1. The paper is well-written, well-motivated, and clearly describes the literature. 
2. The theoretical setup is very clear and readable (except for the experiments section). 
3. The authors provide some empirical evidence that their method is superior to two baseline methods for transferring between regression problems on well-established datasets.

Weaknesses:
My main problem with the paper is the metrics proposed for transferability and their associated generalization bounds. 
he paper defines the transferability of a certain pre-trained model to a downstream task using Defs. 1 and 2. These definitions assert that transferability is possible if training a regularized head on top of the pre-trained model given the available target task's data is possible. 
The main problem I have with Defs. 1 and 2 is that these definitions are uninformative when the target
task's data is small. 

1. There is no guarantee in this paper that the pre-trained model would allow T^{lab}(D_S,D_T) to be small. Why can I trust that if I train on a source task, I would be able to use it to fit the target data? What is the connection between the two tasks? 
If I understand correctly, the paper implicitly assumes that the pre-trained model is sufficiently expressive to allow that. As the authors mention, indeed in practice we use a pre-trained large model (e.g., ResNet-50) which allows T^{lab}(D_S,D_T)/T^{lin}(D_S,D_T) to be small. However, this introduces another problem which is that if the target task's data is small, there is no guarantee that the trained head predictor would not overfit the target task's data. Even if we regularization the top head as suggested by the authors, I believe that it is unclear why it would help avoid overfitting. 

2. These issues are clearly manifested in the bounds proposed in Sec. 3. In Theorem 1 for example, we want Tab^{lab}(D_S,D_T) to be small (e.g., lambda is not too large, the pre-trained needs to be sufficiently expressive) and at the same time, C/sqrt{n_t} needs to be small. Since C measures the complexity of the pre-trained model, it is typically a very large number (depends on the size of the network, including its input dimension, depth, width, etc), while n_t needs to be a small number of samples (<100). It is obvious that increasing lambda cannot resolve this issue. 

3. Another issue I have with the paper is the exposition of the experiments. For example, I feel like the description of the source and target tasks are missing. How many samples per task? How is the performance on each one of them is evaluated? How training is done on each one of them? These details are given implicitly, but I believe that more detail and explanations are necessary. I am not sure I understand the definition of the correlation metric used in Table 1. The authors state "how well our transferability estimators correlate (using Pearson correlation) with the test MSE of the target model obtained from actual transfer learning" but I find it quite vague. Why wouldn't you report the test performance on the target regression problem of the the model?

4. The author compare with two baseline methods. Could the authors provide a brief explanation what they are doing and why we should consider them? 

5. Can the authors apply their method on classification problems by treating the problem as a regression problem with the MSE loss with one-hot labels? If so, how would the performance of the proposed methods compare with standard transfer learning methods for classification? 

Minor issues:
1. In theorem 4 and its proof the authors write n instead of n_t. 

2. Some missing related work:
I think the paper could discuss several other works that are missing from the related work.
a. The authors refer to classic Domain Adaptation papers (e.g., Mansour et al. 2009) but should probably add a reference to Ben David et al. 2007 (https://papers.nips.cc/paper/2006/hash/b1b0432ceafb0ce714426e9114852ac7-Abstract.html).
b. I believe that the authors should address the two papers of Galanti et al. 2022 (https://openreview.net/forum?id=SwIp410B6aQ, https://openreview.net/forum?id=VrK7pKwOhT_) on transfer learning between a source and target classification problems. In these papers, the authors provide generalization bounds for transfer learning algorithms with very few samples for the target task as well as concrete metrics for measuring transferability.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The authors claim that their generalization bounds are novel several times in the paper.
However, I feel like the theoretical results do not provide much insight into transfer learning. 
The results essentially argue that if the model can perform well on the target dataset and the target dataset is large in comparison with the model's size, then the model performs well at test time. This is not a very new argument.
content.summary_of_the_review: I believe that the theoretical aspects of the paper are not very insightful and the experimental evaluations are unclear to me.
content.correctness: 3: Some of the paper’s claims have minor issues. A few statements are not well-supported, or require small changes to be made correct.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper investigated Linear MSE and Label MSE for transferability estimation of regression tasks. The author proved theoretical bounds for the expected risk of the target models using these estimators, for both the general setting and the shared inputs setting. Experiments showed the superiority to prior methods in terms of efficiency and effectiveness.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Pros:  
+ The paper is well written and easy to follow. The authors make good efforts to formalize the problem and introduce the definition of two families of transferability estimators, Linear MSE and Label MSE. Furthermore, the authors prove theoretical bounds connecting Label MSE and Linear MSE with the expected risk of the optimal target models obtained from the actual transfer learning process.

+ The experimental results demonstrate that the proposed method achieves superior performance to some prior methods.

Cons:  
- My main concern lies in the novelty of the work. Both Linear MSE and Label MSE are very straightforward and share the same idea with some prior works like LEEP. The differences in the detailed implementation are not sufficient to turn them into novel methods. The main novelty of the work may lie in the theoretical analysis for the two methods. However, as the two methods are intuitively very sound, the contribution of the theoretical analysis to the field is limited.

- Some highly relevant works are missing from the paper, e,g.,  
[1] Deep Model Transferability from Attribution Maps, NeurIPS2019.  
[2] DEPARA: Deep attribution graph for deep knowledge transferability, CVPR2020.   
The authors are encouraged to clarify the differences from these works or make comparisons in the experiments if possible.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The paper is well written and easy to follow. The proposed methods are technically sound and shown effective in the experiments. However, the novelty of the paper is somewhat limited as the methods share the same main idea with some prior works.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The problem of estimating how well deep neural network regression models would transfer from source to target tasks is explored in this paper. It targets at regression tasks and develops a new method to measure the transferability by MSE loss of a regularized linear regression model based on features or labels. Some theoretical bounds are analyzed, and the method is empirically tested on CUB-200-2011 and OpenMonkey keypoint detection tasks. Experiments are mainly conducted between different keypoints in three transfer learning algorithms (head re-training / half fine-tuning / full fine-tuning). The authors claim a clear improvement over existing state-of-the-art regression task transferability estimators in both accuracy and efficiency.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
# Strength

Indeed the regression problem is less investigated in the literature (only two papers (You et al., 2021) and (Huang et al., 2022)). It is good to have researchers dive into this problem. 

Empirical performance reported in the paper is good.

# Weaknesses

The main weaknesses of this paper is that the method is too trivial. Since it tackles the regression problem, then it just uses the MSE of linear regression as a measure of transferability. For example, in Table 1, head re-training is almost the same as LinMSE. It is no wonder that LinMSE correlates well with head re-training. Therefore, I don't think results in Table 1 are significant. The same applies to the theoretical properties. The fourth page just states that a feasible solution is sub-optimal to the optimal solution, which is very uninformative.

There are in total 4 variants of the proposed method: Lab/Lin MSE 0/1. No suggestions about which one to use and how to set the lambda parameter in practice. 

Some side concerns:
The abbreviation of SotA is strange. The convention is SoTA, I think.

I found one sentence "From the figure, the prediction trends for LogME, LinMSE0, and LinMSE1 are correct, while that of TransRate is not correct." is very confusing. From Figure 3, it seems the prediction trends for LogME is correct (negative trend), while that of TransRate, LinMSE0, and LinMSE1 are not correct (positive trend).

The claim that "those few methods proposed for estimating regression model transferability have so far been either complex and inefficient (You et al., 2021) or ineffective (Huang et al., 2022)" is strange. It contradicts with the claims in these paper (i.e. heavy optimization in (You et al., 2021) and good performance in (Huang et al., 2022)).
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
# Clarity
Good, easy to read.
# Quality and Novelty
Trivial or known conclusions.
# Reproducibility
Code not provided.
content.summary_of_the_review: This paper deals with an important but under-explored problem: transferability estimation methods for regression. However, the method is too trivial (pick a feasible solution out of all solutions) and the theoretical analyses are too weak.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper studies the transferability between regression problems, which is important but under-studied. Specifically, two transferability estimators with theoretical bounds are proposed.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:

1. This paper is well-written and easy to follow

2. The proposed estimators could provide practical value for this problem

3. Empirical results are comprehensive

Weaknesses:

1. While the problem setup (i.e., using the target data to fine-tune the output layers) has been widely studied, it is also quite restrictive (e.g., methods based on domain alignment).

2. I am not very familiar with the literature of \emph{transferability}, but one motivation of this work “computing the MSE of the transferred target model could be expensive if the network architecture of the target regression heads is deep” is not convincing to me, since in the setting of transfer learning, the sample size of target domain is usually small (otherwise transfer learning won’t be necessary).

3. What is the unique aspect of estimating transferability for regression tasks is not clear in this paper. Specifically, what is the difference if I replace the squared loss with other losses (satisfy the triangle inequality in order to make the proof hold)?  

4. How would the transferability estimators motivate practical algorithms (e.g., algorithms that maximize the transferability between domains)? In my opinion, it is not quite a useful technique is it cannot lead to concrete transfer learning algorithms.

Questions:
1. Regarding the Special Case with Same Input Set, feel it becomes a multilabel learning problem. What are the connections here (e.g., [1])? Is it possible to use the theoretical results in multilabel learning (e.g., [2]) to analyze the transferability?

[1] Wang, L., Liu, Y., Qin, C., Sun, G., & Fu, Y. (2020, April). Dual relation semi-supervised multi-label learning. In AAAI. 

[2] Xu, C., Liu, T., Tao, D., & Xu, C. (2016). Local Rademacher complexity for multi-label learning. IEEE Transactions on Image Processing, 25(3), 1495-1507.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The paper is well-written. 
However, the motivations and novelties are not clear enough to me.
content.summary_of_the_review: This work presents an interesting approach to the estimation of transferability between regression tasks. However, given the weaknesses mentioned about, I don't think it is ready to publish in a ML top-tier conference (e.g., ICLR).

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper studies the metric for transferability in regression tasks. The authors find out that the error of regularized linear regression on top of the features of the source model or the dummy label generated by the source model is a good indicator for the final fine-tuning performance. They demonstrate their methods are better than baselines on the CUB-2011 target task.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Measuring transferability without actually tuning the model is an important tool for model selection in transfer learning. Different from previous works on classification tasks, this paper study the transferability in regression setting. 

Weaknesses:   
1.	The theoretical properties in Sec 3 seems trivial. It is obvious that the linear probe error will be larger than the fine-tuning error, but this does not indicate that linear probe error will be proportional to fine-tuning error. Thus, section 3 does not justify the proposed transferability metric.    
2.	Even the proposed transferability metric itself is not novel. Linear probe on top of features is an adaptation method itself. Linear probe on top of dummy labels can be thought of as linear probe on top of features with rank constraint.     
3.	Insufficient empirical validation. The authors only provide CUB-2011 and OpenMonkey results. There are scores of regression tasks in vision. The effectiveness of the proposed method on two tasks is pretty limited.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The paper is overall clearly written.
content.summary_of_the_review: Although the topic is interesting, the quality of the contents is unsatisfactory due to the weaknesses above.
content.correctness: 2: Several of the paper’s claims are incorrect or not well-supported.
